claim: Cytoplasmic dynein uses energy from ATP hydrolysis to move towards the minus ends of microtubules.
source: Cytoplasmic dynein ('dynein' here), the largest and least understood of the cytoskeletal motors, uses the energy from ATP hydrolysis to move towards the minus ends of microtubules (Vale, 2003; Carter, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Vale, 2003 and Carter, 2013

claim: Dynein is the major minus-end-directed motor in most eukaryotic cells.
source: As the major minus-end-directed motor in most eukaryotic cells, dynein's many roles include transporting a range of macromolecular cargo (Blocker et al., 1997; Jordens et al., 2001; Kural et al., 2005; Pilling et al., 2006; Driskell et al., 2007), constructing and positioning the mitotic spindle (Heald et al., 1996; Merdes et al., 1996; Kiyomitsu and Cheeseman, 2013), and polarizing and anchoring mRNAs during development (Wilkie and Davis, 2001).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations describing dynein's cellular roles

claim: Dynein is a homodimer of force generating units, each approximately 500 kDa.
source: Dynein is a homodimer of force generating units (∼500 kDa each) (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 1A,B

claim: The N-terminal region of each dynein monomer forms the 'tail' domain, which mediates dimerization and cargo attachment via adaptor proteins.
source: The N-terminal region of each monomer forms the 'tail' domain, which mediates dimerization and cargo attachment via adaptor proteins.
evidence: Direct statement about dynein structure and function

claim: Removal of the tail yields the 'motor', the minimal portion of dynein that can exert force.
source: Removal of the tail yields the 'motor', the minimal portion of dynein that can exert force.
evidence: Direct statement about dynein motor domain

claim: At the core of the dynein motor are six AAA+ modules (AAA1–6) that fold into a ring.
source: At the core of the motor are six AAA+ modules (AAA1–6) that fold into a ring.
evidence: Direct statement about dynein structure

claim: AAA1 is the main site of ATP hydrolysis for dynein motility.
source: AAA1 is the main site of ATP hydrolysis for motility but AAA2, 3, and 4 can also bind ATP, and AAA3 and 4 can hydrolyze it (Gibbons et al., 1991; Kon et al., 2004, 2012; Cho et al., 2008; Schmidt et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: AAA2, 3, and 4 can bind ATP, and AAA3 and 4 can hydrolyze it.
source: AAA1 is the main site of ATP hydrolysis for motility but AAA2, 3, and 4 can also bind ATP, and AAA3 and 4 can hydrolyze it (Gibbons et al., 1991; Kon et al., 2004, 2012; Cho et al., 2008; Schmidt et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: AAA5 and AAA6 have lost the ability to bind nucleotide.
source: AAA5 and AAA6 have lost the ability to bind nucleotide (Kon et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kon et al., 2012 and Schmidt et al., 2012

claim: The 'stalk' is an intramolecular anti-parallel coiled-coil at the end of which lies the microtubule-binding domain.
source: Two appendages to the ring are essential for dynein function; the 'stalk', an intramolecular anti-parallel coiled-coil at the end of which lies the microtubule-binding domain (Gee et al., 1997; Carter et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to Gee et al., 1997 and Carter et al., 2008

claim: The 'linker' is dynein's key mechanical element and is an elongated structure N-terminal to AAA1.
source: and the 'linker', which is dynein's key mechanical element and is an elongated structure N-terminal to AAA1.
evidence: Direct statement about linker structure and function

claim: The linker spans the ring and moves in a nucleotide dependent manner that is thought to transmit force to dynein's cargo.
source: The linker spans the ring and moves in a nucleotide dependent manner that is thought to transmit force to dynein's cargo (Burgess et al., 2003; Kon et al., 2005; Shima et al., 2006; Roberts et al., 2009, 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: For dynein to move along microtubules, ATP binding/hydrolysis at AAA1 must be coupled with linker motion and microtubule binding and release at the tip of the stalk, located 250 Å away.
source: In order for dynein to move along microtubules, ATP binding/hydrolysis at AAA1 must be coupled with linker motion and microtubule binding and release at the tip of the stalk, located 250 Å away (Gibbons et al., 2005; Imamula et al., 2007; Kon et al., 2009; Redwine et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Lis1 is the only dynein regulator known to interact directly with its motor domain.
source: Lis1 is the only dynein regulator known to interact directly with its motor domain (McKenney et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to McKenney et al., 2010 and Huang et al., 2012

claim: Lis1 acts as a dimer.
source: Like dynein, Lis1 acts as a dimer, with each monomer comprising an N-terminal dimerization domain (LisH) followed by a coiled-coil, a flexible loop and a C-terminal β-propeller domain of 7 WD motifs (Kim et al., 2004; Tarricone et al., 2004) (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kim et al., 2004 and Tarricone et al., 2004, and illustrated in Figure 1A,B

claim: Each Lis1 monomer comprises an N-terminal dimerization domain (LisH) followed by a coiled-coil, a flexible loop and a C-terminal β-propeller domain of 7 WD motifs.
source: Like dynein, Lis1 acts as a dimer, with each monomer comprising an N-terminal dimerization domain (LisH) followed by a coiled-coil, a flexible loop and a C-terminal β-propeller domain of 7 WD motifs (Kim et al., 2004; Tarricone et al., 2004) (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kim et al., 2004 and Tarricone et al., 2004, and illustrated in Figure 1A,B

claim: The propeller domain alone can regulate dynein in vitro.
source: We previously showed that the propeller domain alone can regulate dynein in vitro and used negative stain electron microscopy (EM) and two-dimensional (2D) image processing to show that Lis1 binds to dynein's motor domain near AAA3/4 (Huang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Huang et al., 2012

claim: Lis1 binds to dynein's motor domain near AAA3/4.
source: We previously showed that the propeller domain alone can regulate dynein in vitro and used negative stain electron microscopy (EM) and two-dimensional (2D) image processing to show that Lis1 binds to dynein's motor domain near AAA3/4 (Huang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Huang et al., 2012

claim: Lis1 induces a slow-moving microtubule-attached state in dynein.
source: We and others have shown that Lis1 induces a slow-moving microtubule-attached state in dynein (Yamada et al., 2008; McKenney et al., 2010; Torisawa et al., 2011; Huang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Lis1 can induce a slow-moving microtubule-attached state in dynein without substantially affecting dynein's overall ATP hydrolysis rate.
source: Interestingly, Lis1 can accomplish this without substantially affecting dynein's overall ATP hydrolysis rate (Yamada et al., 2008; McKenney et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Lis1 acts as a 'clutch', uncoupling dynein's engine (AAA+ ring) from its track-binding region.
source: This led us to propose that Lis1 acts as a 'clutch', uncoupling dynein's engine (AAA+ ring) from its track-binding region.
evidence: Authors' interpretation based on previous findings

claim: The 3D structure of the dynein–Lis1 complex shows that binding of Lis1 to dynein's AAA+ ring sterically prevents dynein's linker from completing its normal conformational cycle.
source: The three-dimensional structure of the dynein–Lis1 complex shows that binding of Lis1 to dynein's AAA+ ring sterically prevents dynein's main mechanical element, the 'linker', from completing its normal conformational cycle.
evidence: Based on the 3D EM structure obtained in this study

claim: Eliminating the steric block by shortening the linker to a point where it can physically bypass Lis1 renders single dynein motors insensitive to regulation by Lis1.
source: Single-molecule experiments show that eliminating this block by shortening the linker to a point where it can physically bypass Lis1 renders single dynein motors insensitive to regulation by Lis1.
evidence: Based on single-molecule experiments performed in this study

claim: Lis1 keeps dynein in a persistent microtubule-bound state by directly blocking the progression of its mechanochemical cycle.
source: Our data reveal that Lis1 keeps dynein in a persistent microtubule-bound state by directly blocking the progression of its mechanochemical cycle.
evidence: Conclusion based on combined structural and functional data from this study

claim: Mutations in the Lis1 gene cause the neurodevelopmental disorder lissencephaly.
source: Mutations in the Lis1 gene cause the neurodevelopmental disorder lissencephaly (Reiner et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citation to Reiner et al., 1993

claim: The dynein–Lis1 complex was obtained at a resolution of 21 Å.
source: We imaged dynein–Lis1 and dynein alone in the absence of nucleotide and obtained structures at resolutions of 21 Å for the complex (Figure 1C,E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and Video 1)
evidence: Resolution determined from FSC analysis of EM data

claim: The dynein alone map was obtained at a resolution of 15 Å.
source: and of 15 Å for dynein alone (Figure 1D,F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and Video 2).
evidence: Resolution determined from FSC analysis of EM data

claim: The dynein alone map accommodates the crystal structures of the dynein motor domain well.
source: The dynein alone map accommodates the crystal structures of the dynein motor domain well (Kon et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2012) (Figure 1F), with a Fourier Shell Correlation between the EM map and yeast motor domain structure (Schmidt et al., 2012) of 0.143 at a resolution of 18.8 Å.
evidence: FSC calculation between EM map and crystal structure

claim: The dynein–Lis1 map shows a prominent donut-shaped density in contact with the dynein ring, adjacent to the stalk.
source: The dynein–Lis1 map shows two major differences relative to the dynein alone reconstruction. First, a prominent donut-shaped density is resolved in contact with the dynein ring, adjacent to the stalk (Figure 1C, brown arrowhead).
evidence: Observed in the EM reconstruction

claim: The extra density in the dynein–Lis1 map matches the dimensions of a β-propeller, including the hole at its center.
source: This extra density matches the dimensions of a β-propeller, including the hole at its center (Figure 1E,G,H).
evidence: Comparison of EM density with known β-propeller structure

claim: The donut-shaped density in the dynein–Lis1 map corresponds to Lis1.
source: We thus conclude that the density corresponds to Lis1.
evidence: Inference based on density shape and location

claim: Lis1 binds on the same face of the ring where dynein's linker domain is located.
source: The second, and striking difference between the two maps is in dynein itself: Lis1 binds on the same face of the ring where dynein's linker domain is located and the linker is displaced by ∼44 Å in the dynein–Lis1 map relative to the dynein alone reconstruction (Figure 1C–F).
evidence: Observed in the EM reconstructions

claim: The linker is displaced by approximately 44 Å in the dynein–Lis1 map relative to the dynein alone reconstruction.
source: The second, and striking difference between the two maps is in dynein itself: Lis1 binds on the same face of the ring where dynein's linker domain is located and the linker is displaced by ∼44 Å in the dynein–Lis1 map relative to the dynein alone reconstruction (Figure 1C–F).
evidence: Measured from EM reconstructions

claim: The extra density in the dynein–Lis1 3D map fits well a single homology model of the S. cerevisiae Lis1 β-propeller built from the crystal structure of the mouse protein.
source: The extra density in the dynein–Lis1 3D map fits well a single homology model of the S. cerevisiae Lis1 β-propeller built from the crystal structure of the mouse protein (Tarricone et al., 2004) (Figure 1E,G,H).
evidence: Homology model docked into EM density

claim: The stoichiometry of the dynein–Lis1 complex is one Lis1 propeller to one dynein motor domain.
source: 2D image analysis of dynein–Lis1 complexes with either monomeric or dimeric Lis1 showed the same density and location for Lis1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E), further supporting a stoichiometry of one Lis1 propeller to one dynein motor domain.
evidence: Based on 2D image analysis

claim: The Lis1 β-propeller contacts dynein primarily at a surface-exposed helix at the junction of AAA3 and AAA4.
source: Our structure of the dynein–Lis1 complex shows that the Lis1 β-propeller contacts dynein primarily at a surface-exposed helix at the junction of AAA3 and AAA4 (Figure 2A and Video 3)
evidence: Observed in the EM structure

claim: Mutagenesis of four conserved, charged residues (KDEE) on the AAA3/AAA4 helix virtually abolished Lis1 binding and dynein regulation.
source: explaining why mutagenesis of four conserved, charged residues (KDEE) on this helix virtually abolished Lis1 binding and dynein regulation (Huang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Huang et al., 2012

claim: When all five residues (R275, R301, R378, W419, K437) in Lis1 are mutated to alanine (Lis15A), no binding to dynein could be detected by size-exclusion chromatography.
source: When all five residues are mutated to alanine (Lis15A), no binding could be detected by size-exclusion chromatography (Figure 2C and Table 2).
evidence: Experimental result from size-exclusion chromatography

claim: Lis1R378A and Lis1W419A single point mutants did not show detectable interaction with dynein by size-exclusion chromatography.
source: We also did not detect an interaction with two of the single point mutants, Lis1R378A and Lis1W419A (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Experimental result from size-exclusion chromatography

claim: The remaining single point mutants (R275A, R301A, K437A) showed decreased but detectable binding to dynein.
source: The remaining single point mutants showed decreased but detectable binding to dynein (Table 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Experimental result from size-exclusion chromatography

claim: Highly conserved amino acids on the top face of Lis1's β-propeller are critical for dynein binding.
source: Thus, we conclude that highly conserved amino acids on the top face of Lis1's β-propeller are critical for dynein binding, in support of our structural model for the dynein–Lis1 complex (Figure 2A).
evidence: Conclusion based on mutagenesis data

claim: The Lis15A mutant showed no reduction in dynein velocity in single-molecule assays.
source: The Lis15A mutant showed no reduction in dynein velocity, consistent with an inability to bind dynein (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Experimental result from single-molecule motility assays

claim: The Lis1R378A mutant showed a slight reduction in dynein velocity compared to dynein alone.
source: The Lis1R378A mutant, on the other hand, showed a slight reduction in dynein velocity compared to dynein alone, suggesting that its binding to the motor is compromised (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Experimental result from single-molecule motility assays

claim: Disruption of the dynein–Lis1 interface resulted in a decrease in the number of bud neck crossings to a level similar to that caused by the deletion of Lis1.
source: We found that disruption of the dynein–Lis1 interface resulted in a decrease in the number of bud neck crossings to a level similar to that caused by the deletion of Lis1 (Figure 2E).
evidence: Experimental result from spindle oscillation assays

claim: The dynein–Lis1 interface identified in the structural model is crucial for dynein's biological function.
source: These results indicate that the dynein–Lis1 interface identified in our structural model is crucial for dynein's biological function.
evidence: Conclusion based on in vivo spindle oscillation assays

claim: The linker position in the dynein alone structure is sterically incompatible with the presence of Lis1.
source: The structure suggests that this displacement may be a direct result of Lis1's binding to dynein: the linker position in the dynein alone structure is sterically incompatible with the presence of Lis1 (Figure 1D).
evidence: Observed in the EM structures

claim: In the presence of ADP, the linker adopts two positions: one over AAA4 and one at AAA5.
source: Conformational sorting revealed that the linker adopts two positions in this condition (Figure 3A). One is over AAA4, coinciding with that observed in the D. discoideum crystal structure. The other is the AAA5-docked position seen in S. cerevisiae dynein with no nucleotide.
evidence: Observed in EM reconstructions with ADP

claim: The AAA4 linker position was seen only in the presence of ADP and was not detectable in no nucleotide conditions.
source: The AAA4 position was seen only in the presence of ADP and was not detectable in no nucleotide conditions.
evidence: Comparison of EM reconstructions in different nucleotide states

claim: Both the AAA4 linker position in the ADP state and the AAA5 position in the no nucleotide state are sterically incompatible with the presence of Lis1.
source: Importantly, both the AAA4 linker position in the ADP state and the AAA5 position in the no nucleotide state are sterically incompatible with the presence of Lis1 (Figure 3B).
evidence: Observed by overlaying EM structures

claim: Binding of Lis1 to the dynein ring results in a displaced linker, away from its normal docking sites under both no nucleotide and ADP conditions.
source: Thus, we conclude that binding of Lis1 to the dynein ring results in a displaced linker, away from its normal docking sites under both no nucleotide and ADP conditions.
evidence: Conclusion based on EM structures in different nucleotide states

claim: In the presence of ATP and vanadate (Vi), FRET increased to approximately 26% in the dynein FRET construct.
source: In the presence of ATP and vanadate (Vi), which trap dynein as an ADP.Vi-bound complex after hydrolysis, FRET increased to ∼26% (Figure 3D).
evidence: Experimental result from FRET measurements

claim: When Lis1 was added to ADP.Vi–dynein, there was no significant change in the FRET efficiency relative to ADP.Vi–dynein alone.
source: When Lis1 was added to ADP.Vi–dynein, there was no significant change in the FRET efficiency relative to ADP.Vi–dynein alone (Figure 3D).
evidence: Experimental result from FRET measurements

claim: Lis1 does not affect the linker pre-powerstroke AAA2 position.
source: These results suggest that Lis1 does not affect the linker pre-powerstroke AAA2 position (ATP + Vi added before Lis1) and has only a minor effect on linkers undergoing the AAA5 to AAA2 transition (Lis1 added before ATP + Vi).
evidence: Conclusion based on FRET measurements

claim: The presence of Lis1 does not interfere with linker movement towards its pre-powerstroke position at AAA2.
source: In summary, these results indicate that the presence of Lis1 does not interfere with linker movement towards its pre-powerstroke position at AAA2.
evidence: Conclusion based on FRET and EM data

claim: Lis1 occludes the linker binding sites at its two post-powerstroke positions (AAA4 and AAA5).
source: In contrast, Lis1 occludes the linker binding sites at its two post-powerstroke positions (AAA4 and AAA5).
evidence: Conclusion based on EM structures

claim: Dynein monomers continued to hydrolyze ATP in the presence of Lis1 at levels similar to those of dynein alone.
source: As expected, dynein monomers continued to hydrolyze ATP in the presence of Lis1 at levels similar to those of dynein alone (Figure 4A).
evidence: Experimental result from ATPase assays

claim: ATP hydrolysis was virtually abolished in a construct where AAA1 was rendered hydrolysis-deficient with an E to Q mutation, both in the presence and absence of Lis1.
source: This hydrolysis, however, was virtually abolished, both in the presence and absence of Lis1, in a construct where AAA1, the main site of ATP hydrolysis in dynein (Gibbons et al., 1987), was rendered hydrolysis-deficient with an E to Q mutation in its Walker B motif (Kon et al., 2004) (Figure 4B).
evidence: Experimental result from ATPase assays

claim: An intact ATP hydrolysis site at AAA1 is required for ATPase activity in the presence of Lis1.
source: This result suggests that an intact ATP hydrolysis site at AAA1 is required for ATPase activity in the presence of Lis1.
evidence: Conclusion based on ATPase assays with AAA1 mutant

claim: Dynein carrying an E to Q mutation in the Walker B motif of AAA4 showed a near wild-type ATPase rate with or without Lis1.
source: However, dynein carrying an E to Q mutation in the Walker B motif of AAA4 (Cho et al., 2008) showed a near wild-type ATPase rate with or without Lis1 (Figure 4C).
evidence: Experimental result from ATPase assays

claim: A hydrolysis-competent AAA4 is not required for the ATPase activity observed in the presence of Lis1.
source: Therefore, a hydrolysis-competent AAA4 is not required for the ATPase activity observed in the presence of Lis1.
evidence: Conclusion based on ATPase assays with AAA4 mutant

claim: Dynein constructs carrying the AAA5 mutation did not hydrolyze ATP even in the presence of Lis1.
source: This was not the case; dynein constructs carrying the AAA5 mutation did not hydrolyze ATP even in the presence of Lis1 (Figure 4D).
evidence: Experimental result from ATPase assays

claim: Sustained ATP hydrolysis in a Lis1-regulated dynein requires a hydrolysis-competent AAA1 and a functional linker-docking site at AAA5.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that sustained ATP hydrolysis in a Lis1-regulated dynein requires a hydrolysis-competent AAA1 and a functional linker-docking site at AAA5.
evidence: Conclusion based on ATPase assays with different mutants

claim: A dimeric dynein motor containing a shortened linker shows robust motility properties in in vitro motility assays.
source: A dimeric dynein motor containing this shortened linker shows robust motility properties in in vitro motility assays (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B) (Reck-Peterson et al., 2006).
evidence: Experimental result from motility assays

claim: Monomers with a short linker showed ATPase levels comparable to those seen with a full-length linker.
source: Monomers with a short linker showed ATPase levels comparable to those seen with a full-length linker, both in the context of a wild-type set of AAA+ modules and in the linker docking-deficient AAA5 mutant (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Experimental result from ATPase assays

claim: The short linker construct can bind Lis1 as shown by co-migration in size-exclusion chromatography.
source: As a monomer, the short linker construct can bind Lis1 as shown both by their co-migration in size-exclusion chromatography (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Experimental result from size-exclusion chromatography

claim: The 3D structure of the short linker dynein–Lis1 complex shows the same conformation for the linker in the presence of Lis1 as observed for the full-length linker in the absence of Lis1.
source: Central to our testing the steric block hypothesis, our 3D structure of the short linker dynein–Lis1 complex shows the same conformation for the linker in the presence of Lis1 as we had observed for the full-length linker in the absence of Lis1 (Figure 1, Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Observed in EM reconstruction

claim: In the presence of a full-length linker, Lis1 converted dynein to a state of persistent microtubule attachment.
source: In the presence of a full-length linker, Lis1 converted dynein to a state of persistent microtubule attachment and dynein monomers stayed bound in the presence of ATP for extended periods as previously shown (Figure 5D–F) (Huang et al., 2012).
evidence: Experimental result from microtubule release assays

claim: Shortening of dynein's linker eliminated Lis1's ability to induce a persistent microtubule-bound state.
source: Strikingly, shortening of dynein's linker eliminated Lis1's ability to induce this persistent microtubule-bound state.
evidence: Experimental result from microtubule release assays

claim: Lis1 is not capable of regulating microtubule attachment in the short linker construct.
source: Thus, Lis1 is not capable of regulating microtubule attachment in the short linker construct.
evidence: Conclusion based on microtubule release assays

claim: The data support a steric mode of dynein regulation where Lis1 physically blocks the linker.
source: These data support a steric mode of dynein regulation where Lis1 physically blocks the linker.
evidence: Conclusion based on combined structural and functional data

claim: When Lis1 is present, the linker retains its ability to adopt the pre-powerstroke AAA2 position but is prevented from reaching its normal post-powerstroke positions at AAA4 and AAA5 on dynein's ring.
source: Our data suggest that when Lis1 is present, the linker retains its ability to adopt the pre-powerstroke AAA2 position but is prevented from reaching its normal post-powerstroke positions at AAA4 and AAA5 on dynein's ring (Figure 6).
evidence: Summary of findings from EM and FRET experiments

claim: Blocking of the linker by Lis1 is critical for motility regulation.
source: This blocking of the linker by Lis1 is critical for motility regulation; its removal by shortening dynein's linker renders the motor Lis1 insensitive.
evidence: Conclusion based on short linker experiments

claim: Lis1 may disrupt the interaction between the linker and AAA5, preventing normal progression through the mechanochemical cycle.
source: One possibility suggested by our structures is that Lis1 disrupts the interaction between the linker and AAA5, preventing normal progression through the mechanochemical cycle.
evidence: Speculation based on structural observations

claim: When linker docking at AAA5 is abolished by mutagenesis, dynein displays reduced velocity and prolonged microtubule attachments.
source: Consistent with this notion, when linker docking at AAA5 is abolished by mutagenesis, dynein displays reduced velocity and prolonged microtubule attachments (Schmidt et al., 2012), reminiscent of Lis1's effects.
evidence: Supported by citation to Schmidt et al., 2012

claim: AAA5 linker docking mutants display severely reduced ATPase rates, both in the absence and the presence of Lis1.
source: However, while Lis1 has little effect on dynein's ATPase, AAA5 linker docking mutants display severely reduced ATPase rates, both in the absence (Schmidt et al., 2012) and the presence of Lis1 (Figure 4D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Experimental result from ATPase assays and citation

claim: Low sequence conservation in the portion of the linker facing Lis1 argues against a specific Lis1–linker interaction.
source: Low sequence conservation in the portion of the linker facing Lis1 argues against a specific Lis1–linker interaction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Sequence analysis shown in figure

claim: A specific interaction between a Lis1-displaced linker and dynein's ring is not supported by the apparent conformational heterogeneity of the N-terminus of the linker in the presence of Lis1.
source: Likewise, a specific interaction between a Lis1-displaced linker and dynein's ring is not supported by the apparent conformational heterogeneity of the N-terminus of the linker in the presence of Lis1, where 3D sorting is required to resolve linker positions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: Observed conformational heterogeneity in EM data

claim: Mutating five amino acids on AAA4 proximal to the linker's displaced position had minimal effect on Lis1-mediated motility regulation.
source: Also mutating five amino acids on AAA4, proximal to the linker's displaced position (the most likely candidates to interact with the displaced linker), had minimal effect on Lis1-mediated motility regulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Experimental result from motility assays

claim: Lis1 directly disrupts dynein's mechanochemical cycle by physically blocking conformations that are required to couple the cycles of ATP hydrolysis from those of track binding and release.
source: In conclusion, our data show that Lis1, a conserved dynein regulator, directly disrupts dynein's mechanochemical cycle by physically blocking conformations that are required to couple the cycles of ATP hydrolysis taking place in the motor domain from those of track binding and release happening at the microtubule binding domain.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on all experimental data

claim: Lis1 keeps dynein in a persistent microtubule-bound state.
source: This allows Lis1 to keep dynein in a persistent microtubule-bound state.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental data

claim: The conservation of amino acids at the dynein–Lis1 interface suggests that this modulation of dynein's interaction with its microtubule track contributes to dynein's ability to carry out various cellular functions in different organisms.
source: This modulation of dynein's interaction with its microtubule track likely contributes to dynein's ability to carry out the variety of cellular functions it performs in different organisms, given the conservation of the amino acids at the dynein–Lis1 interface.
evidence: Inference based on sequence conservation

claim: Lis1 is involved in initiation of cargo transport.
source: For example, Lis1 is involved in initiation of cargo transport (Lenz et al., 2006; Egan et al., 2012; Moughamian et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Lis1 is involved in transport of high load cargo.
source: in transport of high load cargo (McKenney et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to McKenney et al., 2010

claim: Lis1 is involved in targeting dynein molecules to the cell cortex via the microtubule plus end.
source: and in targeting dynein molecules to the cell cortex via the microtubule plus end (Lee et al., 2003; Sheeman et al., 2003; Roberts et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: The displaced linker observed in the presence of Lis1 may generate an 'unmasked' tail domain that has been shown necessary for cortical dynein localization.
source: The displaced linker observed in the presence of Lis1 in our 3D dynein–Lis1 reconstruction may contribute to this latter task, generating an 'unmasked' tail domain that has been shown necessary for cortical dynein localization (Markus and Lee, 2011).
evidence: Speculation based on structural observation and citation

claim: Mammalian dynein and Lis1 form a stable complex only in ATP and Vi conditions.
source: In the case of the mammalian proteins, dynein and Lis1 were previously shown to form a stable complex only in ATP and Vi conditions (McKenney et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to McKenney et al., 2010

claim: The stable complex formation between mammalian dynein and Lis1 in ATP and Vi conditions might be a consequence of the linker's moving to its pre-powerstroke site at AAA2, where the linker and Lis1 are no longer sterically incompatible.
source: Our 3D reconstruction of dynein–Lis1 under those conditions suggests that this might be a consequence of the linker's moving to its pre-powerstroke site at AAA2, where the linker and Lis1 are no longer sterically incompatible.
evidence: Inference based on EM structure in ATP+Vi conditions
